title: On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents

paper.title: On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract We study whether small LLM agents can operate effectively under explicit wall-clock time budgets by both respecting the allocated runtime and using available time productively. We evaluate Qwen3.6-27B on five competitions from MLE-Bench Lite and Qwen3-4B on Zork I (Jericho), two agentic benchmarks where additional computational time can meaningfully improve performance. In the simplest setting, where the budget is stated only in the prompt, agents fail to translate the stated budget into controlled use of time. These failures arise from gaps in time awareness, since the harness provides no timing feedback, but also because they cannot reliably anticipate the duration of actions, and do not have a learned mapping from available time to an appropriate strategy. We investigate two complementary classes of interventions: harness-based mechanisms that expose timing information and enforce deadlines, and reinforcement learning with budget-aware rewards. Injecting timing information through the harness substantially improves budget adherence for Qwen3.6-27B without measurable loss in performance, while enforcement hooks tighten adherence further. RL with GRPO achieves near-perfect budget adherence on Zork I and generalizes to held-out budgets not seen during training, but does not improve task performance over the untrained harness on MLE-Bench. Once agents are made to respect the budget, they still fail to use additional time to improve task performance. RL-trained policies learn when to stop but often fill extra time with repeated actions, and GRPO training on multiple budgets tends to collapse toward the strategy learned for the shortest budget. Our results reveal a gap between time adherence and productive time allocation, which remains a central challenge for budget-conditioned agents.

Our results reveal a gap between time adherence and productive time allocation, which remains a central challenge for budget-conditioned agents. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : (Left two) Mean quality (leaderboard percentile) against mean wall-clock time used by Qwen3.6-27B on MLE-Bench, with the budget stated in the prompt (left) and with the enforcement harness added (right). Color gives the stated budget and dashed lines mark the budget values. (Right two) Mid-episode time estimation on 15-minute MLE-Bench tasks. The agent is asked how long it has been working and how long the run will take in total, and its answer is plotted against the true value, with the dashed diagonal marking a perfect estimate. Open markers have a clock in context, filled markers do not. As AI agents take on complex, long-horizon tasks involving planning, tool use, and iterative refinement, how long they spend on a task becomes an important dimension of their behavior, alongside the quality of the final solution. Agents should be able to operate effectively under explicit wall-clock time budgets for two reasons. First, agents face external constraints . A user should be able to control how long a task takes end to end, and an agent embedded in a larger system must meet deadlines to coordinate with other components. Second, for many tasks time is aligned with quality . In search-heavy problems such as ML engineering, more time allows an agent to explore more architectures, hyperparameters, or candidate solutions, so making agents as fast as possible is not the goal. At the same time, users differ in how they weigh solution quality against time, and a time budget is how a user expresses that trade-off. We require two things from an agent operating under a budget, which we call adherence and productive use . Adherence means the agent returns a solution within the allocated time; a harness can force this with a hard interrupt, so that the agent works to the deadline itself. Productive use means the agent spends that time well, using additional budget to improve the solution rather than stopping early or padding its runtime with unnecessary actions. A concrete test is whether task performance improves as the budget increases. If the agent achieves the same quality under a tight budget as under a generous one, the additional time is not being converted into a better solution. Much of these tasks are also dominated by tool call latencies, and we test how well the model is able to take in both the latencies and its generation time in order to stay in budget. Current agents fail at adherence even in the simplest setting, where the budget is stated in the prompt and the harness gives no feedback on elapsed time. On MLE-Bench, Qwen3.6-27B does not use the allocated time effectively (Figure 1 , left; Table 1 ). Qwen3.6-27B runs for roughly ten minutes regardless of the stated budget, overrunning an 8-minute budget while using a small fraction of a 60-minute budget. These failures reflect concrete gaps in what the model can observe and predict about time. Nothing in the model’s context indicates elapsed wall-clock time, and token count is a poor proxy since it depends on hardware and inference configuration. Probing the models directly confirms this. Asked mid-episode how long it has been working, Qwen3.6 27b misjudges its own elapsed time by a large amount on a 15-minute task (Figure 1 , right; Table 9 , Appendix). Agents also cannot reliably predict how long their actions will take, which matters most for long-running tool calls such as training jobs, and even with a clock in context, forecasts of the run’s remaining and total duration stay far off. We hypothesize that even an agent with perfect timing information must still learn to map available time to an appropriate plan. We investigate two complementary classes of interventions: harness-based and learning-based. Harness-based interventions close the observational gaps. A per-action clock and periodic reminders report the remaining budget and the time cost of each action, and an enforcement mode optionally holds the deadline by clamping or refusing over-long commands. Learning-based interventions target the planning gap. We also explore reinforcement learning (GRPO) against budget-aware rewards as a preliminary step toward internalizing the time–quality trade-off directly. We evaluate on two agentic settings where additional time can meaningfully improve outcomes, five competitions from MLE-Bench Lite and Zork I (Jericho), which differ in action structure, feedback density, and how time converts into quality. We select a small number of tasks where different budgets should favor different strategies, and analyze failure modes in detail. In this work, we separate the problem of time budgeting into adherence and productive use, two parts of very different difficulty. We show that adherence is largely solvable in our settings. The harness brings Qwen3.6-27B from 161 % 161\% of budget to on-budget with no measurable loss in quality (between the runs with and without the harness), and RL yields near-exact adherence on Zork I that generalizes to held-out budgets, though training is less effective on MLE-Bench, where the search space is much larger. Productive use , however, is much harder. We show that agents that stay on time do not convert additional time into better outcomes, and the RL policy that learns when to stop fills extra time with actions that do not produce better task results. 2 Related Work Budget-awareness and time-aware test-time scaling. Lin et al. [ 1 ] formalize budget-awareness as progressive interval estimation, where the agent predicts upper and lower bounds on remaining budget at each step, and find that frontier agents are consistently over-optimistic about how much budget remains. Their SFT+RL training improves early-stop behavior, but precise calibration remains difficult. Our work focuses on wall-clock time rather than token budgets, and studies the progression from prompting through harness enforcement to RL rather than a single training method. Li et al. [ 2 ] propose a training-free Budget-Aware Value Tree Search that shifts from exploration to exploitation as budget depletes, and McCleary and Ghawaly [ 3 ] measure how search depth, retrieval strategy, and completion budget affect accuracy under fixed constraints. Both operate at the token or tool-call level. We study wall-clock time, whose stochastic action durations token counting cannot capture. Snell et al. [ 4 ] show that a compute-optimal test-time scaling strategy can outperform a 14 × 14\times larger model, but assume an unlimited budget. Ma et al. [ 5 ] redefine test-time scaling in wall-clock terms with the Timely-Eval benchmark and a Timely-RL training method, and find that existing models fail to adapt reasoning to time budgets. Where Ma et al. focus on a single RL intervention, we compare prompting, harness enforcement, and RL as a progression. Paglieri et al. [ 6 ] use SFT and RL to teach agents when planning is worthwhile. We study how the entire strategy should adapt to a time budget, and find that RL learns when to stop but not what to do differently with more time. Budgeted and constrained reinforcement learning. Constrained Markov Decision Processes [ 7 ] formalize reward maximization subject to cost constraints. Carrara et al. [ 8 ] extend this to Budgeted MDPs, conditioning a single policy on the budget so it solves the CMDP for any budget level without retraining, an idea our RL stage adopts. Our cost signal, wall-clock time, is stochastic and unpredictable, while classical BMDPs assume known cost functions of state-action pairs. McMahan and Zhu [ 9 ] require that the budget never be violated at any point in time, closer to our setting since an agent that overruns at step t t cannot undo it at t + 1 t+1 . Their result that Markovian policies are insufficient under anytime constraints informs our choice to inject remaining budget into the agent’s context. Achille [ 10 ] argues that time is the critical quantity to optimize when scaling reasoning models, and warns of a failure mode in which reward-driven models brute-force solutions without acquiring transferable strategies. Our RL-trained policy’s memorized-prefix-plus-no-ops behavior matches this failure mode. Reinforcement learning for LLMs. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [ 11 ] , introduced for DeepSeek-Math and used for DeepSeek-R1 [ 12 ] , samples a group of rollouts per task and normalizes rewards within the group, avoiding a separate critic network.
